Title: Analog ReLU Activation Enabled by Van Hove Singularities in a Kagome Semiconductor Field‐Effect Transistor

Analog ReLU Activation Enabled by Van Hove Singularities
in a Kagome Semiconductor Field-Eﬀect Transistor
Ziyuan Meng, Hang Xu, Xueli Geng, Zhaoying Ren, Haifeng Feng, Kunrong Du,
Zhijian Shi, Wei Cai,* Zhe Sun,* Hongrun Zhang, Anping Huang, Feng Cheng,
Binghui Ge, Yi Du, and Weichang Hao*
With the growing demand for high-performance computing in deep learning,
energy-eﬃcient analog computing has emerged as a promising alternative to
conventional energy-intensive digital processing. A major obstacle in this ﬁeld
is the physical realization of activation functions, due to the lack of analog
f (FETs) that inherently exhibit the desired piecewise-linear transfer char-
acteristics. Here, a novel strategy is presented for implementing the Rectiﬁed
Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function by exploiting the high density of states
(DOS) associated with van Hove singularities (vHs), induced by ﬂat bands
in a kagome semiconductor Nb3Cl8 FET. This vHs-enhanced DOS imparts
pronounced piecewise-linear transfer behavior at low temperatures, eﬀectively
mimicking the ReLU function. To enable room-temperature operation,
the origin of the hysteresis commonly observed in Nb3Cl8 FETs is identiﬁed
and addressed. Temperature-dependent and time-resolved measurements
attribute the hysteresis to charge trapping at the Nb3Cl8–substrate interface.
By introducing a hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) buﬀer layer, the hysteresis
is successfully suppressed, achieving stable and highly linear transfer
characteristics at room temperature. These results demonstrate the potential
of vHs-engineered electronic states for the physical implementation of
analog activation functions, oﬀering a pathway toward compact, high-density,
and energy-eﬃcient hardware for analog deep learning accelerators.

1. Introduction
The rapid advancement of artiﬁcial in-
telligence (AI) has driven signiﬁcant in-
terest in deep learning across various
ﬁelds in recent years.[1–3] A key com-
ponent of deep learning is the Recti-
ﬁed Linear Unit (ReLU) activation func-
tion, depicted in Figure 1a. Its piecewise-
linear nature ensures computational ef-
ﬁciency and eﬀective gradient propa-
gation, making it highly suitable for
hardware-based implementations. The
ability to physically realize the ReLU
function is particularly critical for neuro-
morphic computing, optical computing,
and analog deep learning accelerators.[4,5]
A ﬁeld-eﬀect transistor (FET), nat-

drain current is eﬀectively suppressed
(Ids ≈0). In contrast, once the gate

comes electron-doped (n-doped), and the transistor operates in
the triode regime (Vds ≪Vg −Vth), where the current follows a
simpliﬁed form of the Shockley equation:

results in a smooth increase in Ids rather than a strictly linear
trend in the FET transfer characteristics (red curves in Figure 1c,
left panel). By contrast, in an ideal 2D semiconductor, the den-
sity of states D(E) exhibits an abrupt increase, causing Ctotal to
transition sharply from zero to CG, provided that CG ≪CQ. Con-
sequently, the transfer characteristics are expected to follow a
more linear trend, with Ids increasing more proportionally with
Vg, closely resembling an ideal ReLU function (blue curves in
Figure 1c, left panel). Recent studies have demonstrated that
FETs based on 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) can
be eﬀectively utilized for implementing ReLU function.[11] An-
other promising approach for achieving a FET with ideal linear
characteristics is to use a semiconductor material exhibiting a
van Hove singularity (vHs), where the DOS increases sharply at
a speciﬁc energy. This phenomenon has been experimentally ob-
served in kagome semiconductors, such as Nb3Cl8. Due to the
signiﬁcantly large DOS associated with the vHs, the Fermi level
remains pinned within the ﬂat band as Vg increases, resulting in
a linear increase in Ids (Figure 1c, middle panel).
In this work, we fabricate a FET using Nb3Cl8 to explore its
potential for realizing the ReLU function. Nb3Cl8 is a van der
Waals (vdW) semiconductor with a frustrated lattice structure
(Figure 1d). In each layer, niobium atoms form a breathing-
kagome lattice, sandwiched between chlorine atoms on either
side (for a detailed crystal structure, see Figure S1a, Support-
ing Information). This breathing-kagome lattice in Nb3Cl8 gives
rise to a ﬂat electronic band, which is intrinsically split into
an upper Hubbard band (UHB) and a lower Hubbard band
(LHB) due to strong electron–electron interactions (Figure 1e).
The presence of vHs in the Hubbard bands has been conﬁrmed
through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES).[12]
Figure 1e presents our ARPES measurement along Γ–M direc-
tion, where the shaded red region highlights the observed ﬂat
LHB with vHs, conﬁrming the electronic structure of our Nb3Cl8
crystal.
Another key factor preventing FETs from exhibiting ideal lin-
ear characteristics is the presence of band-tail states below Ec
(Figure 1c, right panel), which typically arises from parasitic ef-
fects such as interfacial traps. This constitutes the extrinsic cause.
These states broaden the energy distribution of charge carri-
ers, leading to a gradual rather than abrupt transition in car-
rier accumulation. Additionally, interfacial traps can induce hys-
teresis in the transfer characteristics. The presence of hystere-
sis in the transfer characteristics has been reported in Nb3Cl8
FET recently.[13] Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) encapsulation
has been widely employed in the fabrication of vdW materials
to enhance the electronic properties of devices. Its atomically
smooth surface, chemical stability, and ability to suppress charge
inhomogeneities help improve carrier mobility and reduce disor-
der, making it an essential component in high-performance elec-
tronic and optoelectronic applications.[14–16]
Here, we present a h-BN encapsulated, high-quality, gate-
tunable transistor for implementing the ReLU function by ex-
ploiting the high DOS associated with vHs based on the kagome
semiconductor Nb3Cl8. This vHs-enhanced device exhibited im-
proved piecewise-linear transfer characteristics at low temper-
ature (150 K), highly resembling the ReLU function. To facili-
tate room-temperature (RT) operation, we identify the underly-
ing cause of the hysteresis commonly observed in Nb3Cl8 FETs.
The hysteresis is attributed to the charge trapping at the Nb3Cl8–
substrate interface by temperature-dependent and time-resolved
measurements. By introducing a h-BN buﬀer layer, we achieved
hysteresis-free Nb3Cl8 FET with on/oﬀratio close to 103 at RT. As
expected, this device exhibits signiﬁcantly improved piecewise-
linear transfer characteristics, highlighting the impact of the
sharp DOS transition on transistor performance.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Electrical Transport and Hysteresis in Nb3Cl8 FETs on SiO2
Substrates
To investigate the factors contributing to deviations from ideal
linear transfer characteristics in Nb3Cl8 FETs and to imple-
ment the ReLU activation function, we synthesized Nb3Cl8
single crystals and subsequently fabricated Nb3Cl8 FETs. The
crystal structure of the synthesized high-quality 𝛼-Nb3Cl8 sam-
ple was characterized using a combination of X-ray diﬀraction
(XRD), optical microscopy, and scanning transmission electron
microscopy (STEM), as shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Infor-
mation). In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and
energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analysis of Nb3Cl8
revealed an elemental ratio of Nb:Cl = 3:8, consistent with the
expected stoichiometry (see Figure S2, Supporting Information).
The FETs were fabricated directly on SiO2 substrates, using
p-doped Si as the back gate to modulate the carrier density in
Nb3Cl8. Figure 2a displays a schematic illustration and an optical
microscope image of a representative device. After fabrication, we
performed low-temperature transport measurements on a typical
Nb3Cl8/SiO2 FET to investigate its electrical properties. Figure 2b
presents the source-drain current Ids as a function of temperature
during both cooling and heating cycles. A gradual reduction in
current is observed with decreasing temperature, indicating that
Nb3Cl8 behaves as a typical insulator within the investigated tem-
perature range. Figure 2c shows the transfer characteristics of the
Nb3Cl8 FET under bidirectional gate voltage sweeps between −50
and +50 V at various temperatures. At 300 K, the device exhibited
a pronounced clockwise hysteresis. As the temperature decreased
from 300 to 200 K, the hysteresis gradually diminished and even-
tually became nearly negligible at 150 K. This behavior suggests
that the hysteresis eﬀect in the Nb3Cl8 FET is associated with
thermally activated processes and can be eﬀectively suppressed
at lower temperatures.
To harness the intrinsic transport properties of Nb3Cl8, it is
essential to suppress hysteresis. Several mechanisms may con-
tribute to the hysteresis observed in Nb3Cl8 FETs, including in-
trinsic defects in Nb3Cl8, trap states at the Nb3Cl8–SiO2 inter-
face, electron capture and release by surface adsorbates, mo-
bile ions within the SiO2 layer, and charge exchange at the p-
Si–SiO2 interface. These mechanisms are similar to those re-
ported for MoS2 FETs.[17] Among them, hysteresis caused by mo-
bile ions in SiO2 typically manifests as an anti-clockwise hys-
teresis at RT.[18] Hysteresis originating from charge exchange at
the p-Si–SiO2 interface is generally negligible at RT and only
becomes signiﬁcant at elevated temperatures above 350 K, also
in the anti-clockwise direction.[19] Furthermore, reducing the air
pressure at RT did not mitigate the hysteresis (see Figure S3,
Supporting Information), indicating that it is not caused by the

act as charge traps, leading to hysteresis through thermally as-

ature decreases, these thermally activated processes are sig-

hysteresis.
To further analyze the transfer characteristics, we introduce
the transconductance gm, deﬁned as gm = dIds/dVg, as illus-
trated in Figure 2e. For semiconductors with band-tail states,
gm gradually increases toward its expected value (red curve in
Figure 2e, right panel), whereas for semiconductors without
band-tail states, gm exhibits a sharp transition (blue curve in
Figure 2e, right panel). As shown in Figure 2f, the device exhibits
an almost constant transconductance in its n-doped regime, in-
dicating a highly linear transfer characteristic in this region. By
suppressing hysteresis at low temperatures, we reveal that the
improved piecewise-linear transfer characteristic is an intrinsic
property of the hysteresis-free Nb3Cl8 FET. This ﬁnding suggests
that the high DOS associated with vHs is well-suited for imple-
menting the ReLU activation function.

Nevertheless, two challenges remain for practical applications.
First, low temperatures are required to suppress the hysteresis
in the transfer characteristics. Second, the increase in transcon-
ductance in the intermediate region (4 V < Vbg < 17 V) remains
gradual, even at 150 K. Notably, given that the Nb3Cl8 FET ex-
hibits clockwise hysteresis at RT and reduced hysteresis at lower
temperatures, we attribute both issues to interfacial charge traps,
which give rise to band-tail states.
2.2. Electrical Transport in BN-Encapsulated Nb3Cl8 FETs at
Room Temperature
To address the two key challenges, we fabricated Nb3Cl8 FETs
with various device structures and systematically compared
their electrical transport properties. Initially, we prepared a
Nb3Cl8/SiO2 FET, in which Pt/Ti electrodes were deposited on
the top surface of the Nb3Cl8. However, this conﬁguration ex-
hibited non-linear output characteristics due to contact barriers,
preventing the investigation of intrinsic carrier transport prop-
erties (see Figure S4, Supporting Information for the detailed
structure and electrical performance). To realize Ohmic-type con-
tact, we then fabricated an alternative Nb3Cl8/SiO2 FET struc-
ture by placing the Nb3Cl8 ﬂake on top of pre-patterned Pt/Ti
electrodes. This conﬁguration eﬀectively reduced contact resis-
tance. However, signiﬁcant hysteresis persisted in the transfer
characteristics due to interfacial trap states, resulting in a very
low on/oﬀratio (≈2.0) (Figure S5, Supporting Information). To
suppress interfacial trap states, we introduced a h-BN buﬀer
layer between the Nb3Cl8 and the SiO2 substrate, forming a
Nb3Cl8/BN/SiO2 FET. With this structure, the on/oﬀratio im-
proved to ≈26.5 when ∣Vg| < 10 V (Figure S6, Supporting In-
formation). Notably, hysteresis was signiﬁcantly suppressed at
low gate voltages, although it persisted at higher voltages—likely
due to residual traps at the h-BN–SiO2 interface. This obser-
vation was further supported by another Nb3Cl8/BN/SiO2 FET,
which exhibited reduced hysteresis and an enhanced on/oﬀra-
tio of ≈36.7 (Figure S7, Supporting Information). Here, devices
with h-BN buﬀer layers exhibit signiﬁcantly reduced interfacial
trap states, eﬀectively slowing the charge trapping process. This
further enhances ﬁeld-eﬀect modulation, leading to a broader
current range and, consequently, a more pronounced hysteresis
eﬀect.
Based on the above systematic comparison, we conﬁrm that
interfacial trap states between vdW materials and SiO2 substrate
are the primary cause of hysteresis. In the current conﬁguration,
the SiO2 layer serves a dual role: as both the mechanical substrate
and the gate dielectric. To mitigate hysteresis while retaining me-
chanical support, we therefore retained SiO2 solely as the sub-
strate but completed the FET structure by introducing a few-layer
graphite (FLG) top gate with a h-BN dielectric layer.
Figure 3a presents a schematic illustration and an optical
microscope image of the FLG/BN/Nb3Cl8 heterostructure. The
transfer characteristics exhibit negligible hysteresis and a sub-
stantially enhanced on/oﬀratio of up to ≈103 at RT (Figure 3b,
left panel). We also fabricated an additional device with the same
structure, which similarly showed greatly suppressed hysteresis
(Figure S8, Supporting Information). These results demonstrate
that h-BN serves as an excellent dielectric layer for FETs based
on vdW materials. The transconductance exhibits a more abrupt
increase above the threshold voltage compared to the data pre-
sented in Figure 2f, closely resembling a step function (Figure 3b,
right panel). The negative shift in threshold gate voltage suggests
that the Nb3Cl8 crystal is intrinsically n-doped, likely due to the
presence of donor states, as reported in our previous work.[21] To
validate the piecewise-linear behavior, the device was subjected
to three consecutive Vtg sweep cycles, as shown in Figure 3c,
conﬁrming the reliability of the experimental results. We then
extracted the electron mobility µ from the linear regime of the
transfer characteristics using the following relation:[6,22]

An electron mobility of ≈0.014 cm2·V−1·s−1 was obtained for
the Nb3Cl8 sample. This relatively low mobility is consistent
with the high eﬀective mass of electrons, which arises from the
ﬂatness of the Hubbard band. The linear Ids −Vds characteris-
tics conﬁrm the formation of Ohmic contacts in our device, as
shown in Figure 3d. Figure 3e presents the transconductance
curves measured at diﬀerent Vds. In the n-doped regime, the
transconductance increases with increasing bias voltage. This be-
havior corresponds to tuning the slope of the ReLU function—
represented by the parameter 𝛼in Figure 1a. Such slope tuning is
crucial for optimizing the learning dynamics in neural networks,
as it enables precise control over the gradient ﬂow during back-
propagation, which directly impacts the convergence rate and ac-
curacy of training.
According to our experimental results, the hysteresis eﬀect
can be signiﬁcantly suppressed either by employing an appro-
priate dielectric layer, such as h-BN, at RT or by lowering the
temperature. Both approaches mitigate the inﬂuence of inter-
facial trap states. The linear transfer characteristic is attributed
to the high DOS associated with vHs, which distinguishes the
kagome semiconductor Nb3Cl8 from other vdW semiconduc-
tors such as TMDCs.[23–25] Since the Fermi energy shift scales as
ΔEF∝ne/D(EF), where ne is the electron density in the semicon-
ductor, the presence of vHs signiﬁcantly enhances the density of
states D(EF), thereby minimizing the shift in Fermi energy upon
carrier injection. As a result, the Fermi level remains eﬀectively
pinned within the narrow energy window of the ﬂat band, leading
to a linear increase in Ids.
2.3. In Situ Characterization of Interfacial Charge Traps
While h-BN encapsulation eﬀectively suppresses the hysteresis
in transfer characteristics associated with the top gate, the in-
tentional introduction of hysteresis via interfacial traps oﬀers an
intriguing opportunity. This strategy enables the realization of
synaptic transistors with tunable synaptic weights by exploiting
back-gate-induced hysteresis.[26] To elucidate the charge trapping
behavior at the interface between vdW materials and the sub-
strate, we performed time-resolved electrical transport measure-
ments to probe the trapping dynamics, complemented by in situ
Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to spatially resolve sur-
face potential variations induced by localized trapped charges at
diﬀerent interfaces.

Figure 4a illustrates the electron trapping and de-trapping pro-
cesses at the Nb3Cl8–SiO2 interface as the gate voltage Vg in-
creases or decreases. When Vg increases, the electron capture rate
exceeds the emission rate, leading to the accumulation of free
electrons in the trap states until a new equilibrium is established
(Figure 4a, left panel). Conversely, when Vg decreases, the cap-
ture rate becomes lower than the emission rate, and the trapped
electrons are gradually released until the two rates converge
(Figure 4a, right panel).[20] These processes can be detected using
time-resolved electrical transport measurements by applying an
electrical pulse to the gate. Figure 4b shows the time-dependent
response of the drain current Ids for both the Nb3Cl8/SiO2 FET
and the FLG/BN/Nb3Cl8 FET, where the gate is driven by a square
wave with a peak voltage of Vp =
± 10 V. The drain current of
the Nb3Cl8/SiO2 FET exhibits a clear transient response at the
rising and falling edges of the gate voltage pulse (purple curve in
Figure 4b). The rising edge corresponds to the electron trapping
process, while the falling edge corresponds to the de-trapping
process. In contrast, the FLG/BN/Nb3Cl8 FET shows no pro-
nounced transient response (blue curve in Figure 4b), consistent
with our DC transport measurements, which reveal a hysteresis-
free transfer curve at RT (Figure 3b). The transient response en-
ables us to extract the characteristic time scale of the trapping
process at the Nb3Cl8–SiO2 interface, which is ≈4 s.
We next performed in situ KPFM measurements with
nanoscale spatial resolution to map the gate-voltage-dependent
surface potential for Nb3Cl8/SiO2 and Nb3Cl8/BN/SiO2 devices.

3. Conclusion
To summarize, we have demonstrated a novel strategy for phys-
ically implementing the ReLU function by leveraging the high
DOS associated with vHs, induced by ﬂat bands in the kagome
semiconductor Nb3Cl8 FET. The transistor, featuring a vHs,
exhibits a signiﬁcantly improved piecewise-linear transfer be-
havior at low temperatures, highlighting the potential of vHs-
enhanced DOS for realizing activation functions. Temperature-
dependent and time-resolved measurements reveal that the hys-
teresis commonly observed in Nb3Cl8 FETs originates from
trap states at the Nb3Cl8–SiO2 interface. By employing h-BN
as the dielectric layer, we achieved a hysteresis-free top-gated
FLG/BN/Nb3Cl8 FET with stable and highly linear transfer
characteristics, enabling ReLU function implementation at RT.
These results underscore the promise of vHs-engineered elec-
tronic states for the physical realization of analog activation
functions. More broadly, we anticipate that the high DOS aris-
ing from vHs in other vdW semiconductors could similarly
be leveraged to implement the ReLU function in analog com-
puting, thereby paving the way for compact, high-density, and
energy-eﬃcient hardware platforms for analog deep learning
accelerators.
4. Experimental Section
Sample Preparation and Characterizations:
Single crystals of Nb3Cl8
were grown by the solid-state reaction method. Nb (Innochem, 99.95%)
and NbCl5 (Innochem, 99.99%), were mixed at a molar ratio of 7: 8 in the
glove box ﬁlled with argon, and then sealed in a quartz tube under vacuum.
Next, the quartz tube was heated to 817 °C (at the speed of 1 °C s−1) and
kept for 168 h, then naturally cooled to RT to obtain Nb3Cl8 single crystals.
XRD (Panalytical Aeris) with a Cu K𝛼radiation source was used to char-
acterize the crystal structure of Nb3Cl8. The atomic-scale annular dark-
ﬁeld-scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) images of
few-layer Nb3Cl8 samples were performed using a FEI Titan Themis Z mi-
croscope with probe and image correctors operated at 300 kV. The SEM
images and EDX mapping of the Nb3Cl8 ﬂake were acquired using the
JSM-7500F ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscope, coupled with an
EDX system. The topographic mapping and in situ surface potential dif-
ference of the Nb3Cl8 devices were respectively measured by atomic force
microscopy and Kelvin probe force microscopy (Bruker, Dimension Icon)
under ambient conditions, and the gate voltage Vg was applied by a Keith-
ley 6517b electrometer/high-resistance meter. ARPES measurement with
h𝜈= 21.2 eV (He I) at RT was performed in a lab-based ARPES system
equipped with a helium discharge lamp as the light source. The gap be-
tween the Fermi level and valence band is overestimated due to charging
eﬀect caused by the highly insulating behavior of Nb3Cl8.[29]
Preparation
of
Nb3Cl8
FETs:
The
commercial
SiO2/p-Si
and
BN/SiO2/p-Si substrates (heavily p-doped silicon substrates) with
SiO2 layer of 285 nm were used as substrates. For deﬁning the electrodes,
the study employed the maskless photolithography by the lithography
system (Quantum Design, MicroWriter ML3 Lithography Systems) on
the substrates with double-layer photoresist using LOR10A resist and
S1805 positive photoresist. The Pt/Ti (20 nm/5 nm) electrodes were
deposited by magnetron sputtering method, followed by the ultrasonic
cleaning in acetone for 5 min to remove the double-layer photoresist.
Then the residual deposition dissolved in N-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP) for
10 min, followed by ethanol rinsing and drying. Subsequently, the Nb3Cl8
FETs were fabricated by vacuum-assisted dry release transfer method in
a glove box containing argon with 2D material transfer system (Zhuoling
Precision Equipment Co., Ltd). The few-layer Nb3Cl8 ﬂake was prepared
on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) (mass ratio 10:1) sheet by mechanical
exfoliation from an as-grown Nb3Cl8 single crystal using blue adhesive
plastic ﬁlm. Next, the relative positions of Nb3Cl8 ﬂake on PDMS and
electrodes on the SiO2/p-Si substrate were aligned under the optical
microscope observation of the transfer system. The pressure was then
brought to approximately 3.4 × 10−3 Pa through the molecular pump
(Pfeiﬀer vacuum, Hicube Eco Series). Once the ﬂake and substrate with
electrodes come into contact, the substrate stage was heated to 80 °C,
and kept for 5 min. Then, the PDMS and substrate were slowly separated
by moving the substrate stage, and the Nb3Cl8 ﬂake was deposited on the
electrodes of substrate. Similarly, the h-BN layers and graphite layers were
transferred onto the substrates using the same method until diﬀerent
structures of Nb3Cl8 FETs were fabricated for transport measurements.

Electrical Transport Measurements:
The electrical characterization was
carried out by the combination of a Keithley 2400s source measure unit
and a Keithley 6517b electrometer/high-resistance meter, and they share
the same grounds. The Keithley 2400s source measure unit was used to
apply the source-drain voltage (Vds) and measure the source-drain current
(Ids), while the Keithley 6517b electrometer/high-resistance meter was
used to apply the gate voltage (Vg). A four-needle probe station (PSAIC-
Swin, EPS4) was used to measure the FETs at RT, while a physical property
measurement system (Quantum Design, PPMS-14T-DynaCool) was used
to provide the vacuum condition and low-temperature condition for mea-
surements.
DFT Calculations:
The ﬁrst-principle calculations were performed by
using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) with the projec-
tor augmented wave approach and the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE)
generalized-gradient approximation.[30,31] The cut-oﬀenergy of the plane-
wave expansion of the basic functions was set to 350 eV with the preci-
sion of the electronic loop maintained at 1 × 10−6 eV. A 9 × 9 × 3 (5 ×
5 × 2) Γ-centred Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was used to sample the
Brillouin zone for Nb3Cl8. The crystal lattice parameters and positions of
the atoms were optimized with the DFT-D3 vdW correction to a maximum
force of less than 0.01 eV/Å for Nb3Cl8. In order to simulate the Mott phase
in Nb3Cl8, the interlayer antiferromagnetic (AFM) order was set with the
Hubbard U method[32] taking Ueﬀ= 2 eV for Nb d orbital.
